molecules.simple: The most common fever-and-pain medicine. It works on the brain's heat centre to bring a temperature down, and dulls pain signals so aches feel less. It does not reduce swelling.
molecules.how: Adults usually take 500–650 mg with water every 6 hours, after food. Never take more than 3 grams (about 4 tablets) in a day, and avoid alcohol with it — extra doses harm the liver.
watch: Rarely nausea or a skin rash
molecules.alert: See a doctor if fever lasts beyond 3 days, or if you notice yellow eyes/skin, dark urine or severe tiredness — these can signal liver trouble.

molecules.simple: A painkiller of the NSAID family that reduces pain, fever AND swelling. It blocks body chemicals (prostaglandins) that cause inflammation at an injury site.
molecules.how: Take 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours, always after food or with milk — on an empty stomach it can irritate the stomach lining. People with kidney disease, ulcers or dengue should avoid it.
molecules.alert: Stop and see a doctor if you pass black stools, vomit blood, or have severe stomach pain — signs of stomach bleeding.

molecules.simple: A strong anti-inflammatory painkiller for injuries, arthritis and back pain. Like ibuprofen it blocks prostaglandins, the chemicals that make tissue swollen and painful.
molecules.how: Tablets are taken after food (50 mg up to three times a day); the gel is rubbed on the painful area 3–4 times a day. The injection is given by hospital staff only.
watch: Raised blood pressure with long use
molecules.alert: Long use can harm kidneys and stomach — never self-take for more than 5 days. Black stools or vomiting blood means urgent medical care.

molecules.simple: A modern cousin of diclofenac used for arthritis and joint pain. It calms inflammation with, for many people, slightly gentler effects on the stomach than older NSAIDs.
molecules.how: Usually 100 mg twice a day after food. Take the smallest dose that works, for the shortest time.
molecules.alert: Avoid in active stomach ulcers, severe heart failure or kidney disease; report black stools immediately.

molecules.simple: A long-acting NSAID painkiller — one dose works for about 12 hours, so it is often chosen for period cramps and arthritis that trouble you through the day.
molecules.how: 250–500 mg twice a day with food. For period pain it is often started at the first sign of cramps.
watch: Ring in the ears at high doses
molecules.alert: Avoid with stomach ulcers, heart failure or kidney problems. Report black stools or breathlessness.

molecules.simple: An NSAID painkiller especially trusted for period pain and childhood fevers. It works at the site of pain and also directly lowers fever.
molecules.how: 500 mg up to three times a day after food for adults; the syrup dose for children is by weight. Best not used for more than 7 days at a stretch.
molecules.alert: Avoid in the last 3 months of pregnancy and in kidney disease. Very severe cramps that don't settle need a gynaecologist's check.

molecules.simple: A powerful short-course painkiller, close to morphine in punch, used for severe pain like kidney stones or after operations. It is only for a few days, never long-term.
molecules.how: 10 mg every 4–6 hours, with food, for at most 5 days in total. Hospital injections are given into muscle or vein.
molecules.alert: It must never be used with other NSAIDs or before major surgery. Bleeding, black stools or reduced urination need a doctor right away.

molecules.simple: A selective anti-inflammatory painkiller designed to spare the stomach — it blocks the inflammation chemical (COX-2) while mostly leaving the stomach-protecting one (COX-1) alone.
molecules.how: 60–120 mg once a day, with or without food. Gout flares usually take 90–120 mg briefly.
watch: Raised blood pressure with long use
molecules.alert: Not for people with uncontrolled high BP, heart disease or active ulcers. Chest pain or breathlessness while on it needs urgent care.

molecules.simple: Another stomach-friendlier COX-2 anti-inflammatory, used for arthritis pain that swells and stiffens joints. Taken as a capsule once or twice a day.
molecules.how: 100–200 mg once or twice daily with food. Sulfa-allergic people should avoid it.
molecules.alert: Avoid after bypass heart surgery and in serious heart or kidney disease. Report chest pain or sudden weakness.

molecules.simple: The classic pain and fever tablet, and the same family that thins blood. For pain it is used occasionally; the low 75–150 mg dose (see Heart section) is a daily heart medicine.
molecules.how: One 325 mg tablet with food and plenty of water, up to 3–4 times a day at most. Never give to children with fever — it can cause Reye's syndrome, a rare liver-brain illness.
molecules.alert: Avoid in dengue, ulcers, bleeding disorders and before surgery. Ringing ears or black stools mean stop and call a doctor.

molecules.simple: A fast-acting anti-inflammatory painkiller common in India for short-term pain. It is effective but has strict rules: short courses only, and never in children under 12.
molecules.how: 100 mg twice a day after food, for a maximum of 5–7 days. It is banned for children in many countries and should never be used long-term.
molecules.alert: Yellow urine, dark stools or rash means stop immediately and see a doctor — it can, rarely, injure the liver.

molecules.simple: A once-a-day NSAID for arthritis and stiff joints, also available as a gel to rub over aching knees or shoulders.
molecules.how: One 20 mg capsule daily with food, or gel rubbed 2–3 times a day. Long-term use needs monitoring.
molecules.alert: Higher stomach-bleeding risk than many NSAIDs in the elderly — black stools mean stop and seek care.

molecules.simple: An opioid-family painkiller for moderate to severe pain that ordinary painkillers cannot touch. It works on the brain's pain pathways and also lifts pain tolerance.
molecules.how: 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours as prescribed. It can cause sleepiness — do not drive — and it is habit-forming with long use, so it is always time-limited.
molecules.alert: Never mix with alcohol or sleeping tablets. Confusion, very slow breathing or seizures need emergency care.

molecules.simple: A newer opioid-family painkiller for strong pain, acting on pain signals in the brain and spinal cord. Reserved for when milder painkillers have failed.
molecules.how: 50–100 mg as prescribed, usually twice a day for the SR form. Sleepiness is common — driving is unsafe — and long use can cause dependence.
molecules.alert: Do not combine with alcohol or sedatives. Very slow breathing is an emergency.

molecules.simple: A muscle relaxant — it loosens muscles that have gone into painful spasm after a strain, so the underlying painkiller can work better.
molecules.how: 4–8 mg two to three times a day for a few days, usually alongside a painkiller. Can cause loose stools and sleepiness.
molecules.alert: Avoid in pregnancy. If muscle weakness or very loose stools appear, stop and inform your doctor.

molecules.simple: A muscle relaxant that works through the spinal cord to calm over-tight muscles — used after injuries and in neurological conditions with stiffness.
molecules.how: 2 mg at bedtime or up to three times a day as prescribed; it lowers blood pressure slightly, so stand up slowly.
molecules.alert: Never stop it suddenly after long use. Yellowing of eyes or extreme fatigue needs a liver check.

molecules.simple: A wintergreen-scented rub that creates warmth on the skin and distracts pain nerves — the classic Indian pain balm for sore muscles, stiff neck and headaches at the temples.
molecules.how: Massage a small amount over the painful area 2–3 times a day. Never apply to broken skin, and never swallow — it is poisonous by mouth.
molecules.alert: Stop if a rash or blistering appears. Keep away from children — swallowing balm is a medical emergency.

molecules.simple: A penicillin-family antibiotic that punches holes in bacterial walls so germs burst. It is the workhorse for throat, ear, chest and dental infections.
molecules.how: 500 mg every 8 hours as prescribed — and always finish the full course even if you feel better in 2 days, or the infection returns stronger.
molecules.alert: Penicillin allergy is serious: any swelling of lips/face or difficulty breathing after a dose is an emergency. Rash with fever needs a doctor's review.

molecules.simple: Amoxicillin plus a shield-breaker (clavulanic acid) that disables the enzymes resistant bacteria use against it. Used when plain amoxicillin would fail.
molecules.how: 625 mg every 8 hours or 1 g every 12 hours, taken at the START of a meal to prevent stomach upset. Complete the full course.
watch: Thrush in the mouth with long courses
molecules.alert: Stop and report immediately if a deep rash, yellowing of eyes or severe watery diarrhoea appears.

molecules.simple: A 3-to-5-day antibiotic that lingers in tissues, so one dose a day is enough. It gathers inside cells where many common germs hide.
molecules.how: 500 mg once daily for 3–5 days, one hour before or two hours after food (antacids block its absorption).
molecules.alert: Tell your doctor about any irregular heartbeat feeling — rare but reported. Overuse has made many germs resistant; never self-start it for viral fever.

molecules.simple: A third-generation cephalosporin — a broad antibiotic often chosen for urinary infections, typhoid and stubborn throat infections.
molecules.how: 200 mg twice a day (or 400 mg once) as prescribed, with the course always completed.
molecules.alert: Rash, fever with blistering, or blood in stool during the course needs immediate medical review.

molecules.simple: A strong cephalosporin antibiotic good for respiratory infections, sinusitis and skin infections, taken twice daily.
molecules.how: 250–500 mg every 12 hours with food, for the full prescribed course (usually 5–10 days).
molecules.alert: Penicillin/cephalosporin allergy can cross-react — any facial swelling or wheeze is an emergency.

molecules.simple: An oral cephalosporin for respiratory, urinary and skin infections — often picked when a twice-a-day broad antibiotic is needed.
molecules.how: 200 mg every 12 hours with food to boost absorption.
molecules.alert: Severe diarrhoea during or after the course can signal C. difficile infection — see a doctor rather than self-treating.

molecules.simple: A first-generation cephalosporin that is especially good against skin and soft-tissue germs like streptococcus and staphylococcus.
molecules.how: 500 mg every 6–12 hours as prescribed; complete the whole course.
molecules.alert: Allergic swelling or rash needs urgent care; tell your doctor of any penicillin allergy first.

molecules.simple: A powerful injectable antibiotic given only in hospitals and clinics — the backbone of treatment for serious infections like pneumonia, typhoid and sepsis.
molecules.how: Given into a vein or muscle by medical staff, once or twice daily. Courses run several days depending on the infection.
molecules.alert: Tell staff about prior antibiotic allergies. Rash with breathlessness during the drip is an emergency.

molecules.simple: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic that interferes with bacterial DNA copying. Widely used for urinary and stomach infections; the drops treat eye and ear infections.
molecules.how: 500 mg twice daily; doses are spaced from dairy, antacids and iron (they lock to it). Finish the full course.
molecules.alert: Stop and call a doctor at once if a tendon (especially Achilles) starts aching or popping — fluoroquinolones can injure tendons. Not first-line in children.

molecules.simple: A once-daily fluoroquinolone for chest, sinus and urinary infections — the left-handed mirror of ciprofloxacin with better lung coverage.
molecules.how: 500 mg once daily, plenty of water, away from antacids and iron tablets by 2 hours.
molecules.alert: Same tendon and heart-rhythm cautions as ciprofloxacin. Blood sugar can swing in diabetics — monitor.

molecules.simple: A fluoroquinolone that concentrates in the urine — the classic tablet for urinary tract infections and traveller's diarrhoea.
molecules.how: 400 mg twice daily, an hour before or two hours after meals, with lots of water; avoid milk/antacids around the dose.
molecules.alert: Tendon pain or swelling means stop the drug and call your doctor. Avoid in children and pregnancy.

molecules.simple: A tetracycline antibiotic that stops bacteria making proteins. It doubles as an anti-malarial prophylaxis and treats several tick-borne and skin conditions.
molecules.how: 100 mg once or twice daily with a full glass of water, sitting upright; never take just before lying down or with milk (it binds calcium and iron).
molecules.alert: Severe heartburn or pain on swallowing means stop and consult. Use strong sunscreen on treatment.

molecules.simple: A tetracycline cousin used mainly for stubborn acne and some resistant infections; it reaches oily skin and glands well.
molecules.how: 50–100 mg once or twice daily as prescribed, with water and not with milk; courses for acne run weeks to months under supervision.
watch: Blue-grey skin tint with very long use
molecules.alert: Headache with blurred vision (raised pressure) or a drug rash needs urgent review.

molecules.simple: An antibiotic that kills anaerobic germs (those that live without oxygen) and certain parasites. Famous rule: absolutely no alcohol during it and for 2 days after.
molecules.how: 400 mg two or three times daily after food as prescribed; the gel treats rosacea/vaginal infections locally.
molecules.alert: Alcohol causes violent flushing and vomiting with this drug. Numbness or tingling in limbs on long courses must be reported.

molecules.simple: A longer-acting metronidazole relative for anaerobic germs and parasites — often a shorter, simpler course.
molecules.how: As prescribed, commonly 1–2 g once daily after food for 2–3 days, or 500 mg twice daily. Same strict no-alcohol rule.
molecules.alert: Alcohol interaction is as severe as metronidazole. Report numbness or seizures.

molecules.simple: An antibiotic for anaerobic and staph germs, used orally for dental and bone infections and as a gel for acne.
molecules.how: 150–300 mg every 6–8 hours with a full glass of water; apply a thin acne gel layer at night.
molecules.alert: Watery, frequent diarrhoea during or weeks after the course can mean C. difficile colitis — needs prompt treatment, not just an antidiarrhoeal.

molecules.simple: A last-line-class oral antibiotic for resistant gram-positive germs — especially MRSA — used when ordinary antibiotics have failed.
molecules.how: 600 mg every 12 hours as prescribed; courses are monitored with blood counts if longer than 10–14 days.
molecules.alert: It interacts dangerously with antidepressants and aged cheese (serotonin surge): agitation, sweating, racing heart — call your doctor. Vision changes on long courses need eye checks.

molecules.simple: Two antibiotics in one (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim) that block bacteria's folic-acid factory in different spots — a strong double-lock.
molecules.how: One DS tablet twice daily as prescribed, with plenty of fluids.
molecules.alert: Sulfa allergy can be severe — blistering rash or mouth ulcers mean stop immediately. It interacts with warfarin (bleeding risk) and methotrexate.

molecules.simple: A urinary-specialist antibiotic that concentrates only in urine — effective for simple bladder infections while barely touching the rest of the body.
molecules.how: 100 mg twice daily for 5–7 days with food. Not used for kidney infections (it doesn't reach deep tissue).
molecules.alert: Avoid in significant kidney impairment. Breathlessness or cough during long courses must be reported — rare lung effects.

molecules.simple: A cornerstone anti-TB antibiotic that shuts down bacterial RNA production. It turns urine, sweat and tears orange-red — harmless and expected.
molecules.how: Always in combination with other TB drugs, taken on an empty stomach in the morning, daily for months as directed.
molecules.alert: It weakens many medicines — birth-control pills, warfarin, diabetic drugs. Yellow eyes, severe fatigue or vomiting need a liver check urgently.

molecules.simple: The other pillar of TB treatment, blocking mycolic acid that builds the TB bacterium's wall. Taken daily for months with vitamin B6 cover.
molecules.how: 300 mg once daily on an empty stomach, usually with pyridoxine (B6) to protect nerves; never taken alone for active TB.
molecules.alert: Yellowing of eyes, dark urine or persistent vomiting means possible liver injury — stop and see your doctor immediately.

molecules.simple: An anti-TB drug that stops the bacterium building its cell wall. Its famous side effect is on eyesight, so vision is checked before and during treatment.
molecules.how: Weight-based dose (15–25 mg/kg) once daily with the rest of the TB regimen.
molecules.alert: Any change in vision or colours — report the same day; stopping early usually protects sight.

molecules.simple: The TB drug that clears bacteria hiding in acidic pockets inside the body, letting treatment courses be shortened to six months.
molecules.how: Weight-based dose once daily with the TB regimen; liver tests are monitored during therapy.
molecules.alert: Yellow eyes, dark urine, severe fatigue or vomiting = possible liver injury, needs immediate review.

molecules.simple: An oral penem antibiotic used in India for resistant respiratory and ENT infections when first-line drugs haven't worked.
molecules.how: 200 mg two or three times daily as prescribed, course completed fully.
molecules.alert: Rash or allergic swelling needs immediate stop-and-review. Not for trivial colds — resistance matters.

molecules.simple: An aminoglycoside 'big gun' injectable for serious hospital infections and resistant TB, given under close monitoring because of kidney and hearing effects.
molecules.how: Given by injection once daily, dose adjusted to kidney function and drug levels.
watch: Ringing in ears or hearing dip
molecules.alert: Any hearing change or reduced urination during the course must be reported immediately — effects can be permanent if ignored.

molecules.simple: A hospital intravenous combination — a broad penicillin with a beta-lactamase shield — used for serious abdominal, lung and blood infections.
molecules.how: Given by drip every 6–8 hours by hospital staff, dose adjusted for kidney function.
molecules.alert: Allergic reactions need immediate staff attention; prolonged courses watch for fungal superinfection.

molecules.simple: A proton-pump inhibitor — it switches off the stomach's acid pumps at the source, so reflux burns less and ulcers can heal. Strongest class of antacid medicine.
uses: With painkiller courses to protect stomach
molecules.how: One 40 mg tablet on an EMPTY stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast — timing decides how well it works. Courses run 2–8 weeks.
molecules.alert: Don't take for years without review — long use can lower B12, magnesium and bone strength. Black stools or coffee-ground vomit is an emergency regardless.

molecules.simple: The original acid-pump switch-off capsule, used for heartburn, ulcers and to protect the stomach during painkiller courses.
molecules.how: 10–20 mg before breakfast, capsule swallowed whole (it's coated to survive stomach acid).
molecules.alert: Review long courses with a doctor. Severe chest pain always needs urgent care — don't assume it's just acidity.

molecules.simple: A fast-acting acid-pump blocker, often paired with domperidone in one capsule for reflux that comes with bloating and slow stomach emptying.
molecules.how: 20 mg once daily before breakfast; the DSR form is taken before breakfast too.
molecules.alert: Pregnancy-safe alternatives should be discussed. Any alarm signs — weight loss, black stools, vomiting blood — need endoscopy, not self-treatment.

molecules.simple: The refined left-handed form of omeprazole — same acid-pump shutdown, chosen for stubborn reflux and erosive ulcers.
molecules.how: 20–40 mg once daily before food, swallow whole.
molecules.alert: Long-term use needs periodic review. Worsening swallowing difficulty or weight loss needs a doctor promptly.

molecules.simple: A stomach-movement booster — it tightens the valve between stomach and food pipe and speeds emptying, so food and acid move downward instead of up.
molecules.how: 10 mg up to three times daily, 15–30 minutes BEFORE meals. Best used for short periods.
molecules.alert: Avoid with heart-rhythm problems and some antibiotics (it can lengthen the QT interval). Not for long unsupervised use.

molecules.simple: The go-to anti-vomiting medicine — it blocks serotonin signals in the gut and brain's vomit centre. Works for chemotherapy, post-op, gastroenteritis and motion sickness rescue.
molecules.how: 4–8 mg up to three times daily; MD tablets melt on the tongue — handy when the patient can't keep water down.
molecules.alert: Tell your doctor if the heart feels fluttery (QT effect with other drugs). Persistent vomiting beyond 24 hours needs assessment for dehydration.

molecules.simple: An older acid-reducer that blocks histamine's acid signal. Many countries have recalled it over impurity concerns, so doctors now usually pick a PPI instead.
molecules.how: 150 mg once or twice daily; if it is prescribed at all, it's usually short-term.
molecules.alert: Ask your doctor about newer alternatives. Any chest pain must be medically assessed, not treated as acidity.

molecules.simple: A histamine-blocker acid reducer — milder than PPIs, good for occasional night-time heartburn without switching the pumps fully off.
molecules.how: 20 mg once or twice daily; onset within an hour. Dose reduced in kidney disease.
molecules.alert: Frequent heartburn most days for weeks needs an endoscopy discussion, not endless self-treatment.

molecules.simple: A stomach bandage — it forms a protective paste that sticks over ulcers and raw patches, shielding them from acid while they heal.
molecules.how: 1 g four times a day on an empty stomach, taken at least 30 minutes BEFORE other medicines (it can block their absorption).
molecules.alert: Not absorbed much, so gentle — but in kidney failure aluminium can build up; use only under advice.

molecules.simple: Classic antacid liquid — aluminium gel soaks up acid while magnesium hydroxide neutralises it instantly. The minty 'chalk' that ends a heartburn episode in minutes.
molecules.how: 10–20 ml after meals and at bedtime, or when burning starts; chewable forms are chewed then followed with water.
molecules.alert: Frequent daily antacid use for weeks hides real ulcers — get checked. Keep 2 hours between antacids and other medicines.

molecules.simple: A fast fizzing antacid — bicarbonate meets stomach acid and releases gas, ending heartburn within minutes. A rescue remedy, not a daily medicine.
molecules.how: Stir one sachet in water and drink after it fizzes; occasional use only.
molecules.alert: High-salt content — avoid in high BP, kidney and heart disease unless advised. Daily heartburn needs a proper evaluation.

molecules.simple: An anti-spasmodic that relaxes cramping gut muscle — the standard tablet for gripping abdominal pain and period-like gut cramps.
molecules.how: 10–20 mg up to four times a day as needed. It dries the mouth slightly and can blur vision briefly.
molecules.alert: Severe abdominal pain should be examined first — spasmodics can mask appendicitis. Glaucoma patients should avoid it.

molecules.simple: A gut-specific anti-spasmodic for IBS — it acts directly on colon muscle without the dry-mouth effects of older spasmodics.
molecules.how: 135 mg three times daily, ideally 20 minutes before meals.
molecules.alert: IBS should be diagnosed by a doctor first — weight loss or bleeding is never IBS.

molecules.simple: An anti-motility medicine that slows the bowel so stools firm up. For simple acute diarrhoea rescue — but it must never be used when there is fever or blood in the stool.
molecules.how: 2 mg after each loose stool, maximum 8 mg/day for 2 days, with ORS fluids in between.
molecules.alert: Never in dysentery (blood/fever) — locking toxins inside worsens illness. Abdominal swelling with no stool means stop and seek care.

molecules.simple: The world's most lifesaving sachet — a precise sugar-salt mix that pulls water back into the body through the gut lining, replacing what diarrhoea steals.
molecules.how: Dissolve one sachet in exactly 1 litre of clean water (not milk/juice), sip continuously; children take small sips every few minutes. Make a fresh batch every day.
molecules.alert: Signs of dehydration — no urine for 8 hours, sunken eyes, drowsiness, cold hands — need hospital care, not just ORS.

molecules.simple: A sugar the human gut can't digest — bacteria ferment it, pulling water into the stool and softening it naturally over 1–2 days.
molecules.how: 15 ml at bedtime, adjustable up to twice daily; drink extra water. Effect builds over a couple of days.
molecules.alert: Very sticky sweetness — diabetics should use under advice. No stool plus vomiting and pain means obstruction — hospital now.

molecules.simple: A two-way laxative: magnesium salts pull water into the bowel while paraffin lubricates the stool so it slides out easily by morning.
molecules.how: 10–30 ml at bedtime with water; keep well hydrated. Rescue use for a few days, not a daily habit.
molecules.alert: Daily laxative dependence should be reviewed. Sudden constipation with vomiting and pain is an emergency.

molecules.simple: Natural fibre husk that swells into a soft gel in the gut — it bulks loose stools AND softens hard ones, the gentle regulator for daily bowel care.
molecules.how: 1–2 teaspoons in a full glass of water at bedtime, drunk immediately before it gels — followed by more water.
watch: Needs lots of water or it can firm up instead
molecules.alert: Never take it dry. Swallowing difficulty or unexplained weight loss needs medical review, not just fibre.

molecules.simple: A 'friendly bile acid' that makes bile less stone-forming and shields liver cells — used for gallstones (chosen cases) and itchy liver conditions in pregnancy.
molecules.how: 8–15 mg/kg per day in divided doses, or as directed; gallstone therapy runs 6–12 months with ultrasound checks.
molecules.alert: Gallstone attacks (right-upper-belly pain after fatty meals) still need surgical opinion — tablets don't fix a blocked stone.

molecules.simple: A beneficial yeast that crowds out harmful germs and steadies the gut lining — added to diarrhoea treatment to shorten the loose-stool days.
molecules.how: One sachet/capsule once or twice daily during the episode; can continue a few days after stools normalise.
molecules.alert: Avoid in severely immunosuppressed patients and central lines — rare fungal spread. Persistent diarrhoea beyond 3 days needs evaluation.

molecules.simple: A mix of friendly Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium bacteria that re-balances gut flora after antibiotics or infection.
molecules.how: One capsule/sachet once or twice daily, ideally spaced 2–3 hours from the antibiotic dose.
molecules.alert: Immunocompromised patients should ask their doctor first. Severe bloody diarrhoea needs a physician, not probiotics.

molecules.simple: An osmotic laxative — long sugar chains hold water in the stool mechanically (no stimulant cramping), making it the preferred gentle daily softener.
molecules.how: One sachet dissolved in a glass of water, once daily; effect in 1–3 days. Adjust dose to stool softness.
molecules.alert: Severe abdominal pain or no gas passing means obstruction — emergency. Heart/kidney failure patients use under advice.

molecules.simple: The first-line sugar medicine worldwide. It tells the liver to release less glucose and helps the body respond to its own insulin — it does NOT force the pancreas to pour out insulin.
molecules.how: Taken WITH meals to ease stomach effects; the SR form is once daily in the evening. Never skip meals on it — combine with the doctor's diet plan.
molecules.alert: STOP before any contrast CT scan or if severely dehydrated/vomiting — rare lactic acidosis risk. Kidney function is checked periodically.

molecules.simple: A sulfonylurea that nudges the pancreas to release more insulin. Effective and cheap — but because it pushes insulin regardless of meals, low-sugar episodes are its main risk.
uses: Combined with metformin when sugar stays high
molecules.how: One tablet with breakfast daily — skipping that meal after taking it invites hypoglycaemia. Carry sugar/glucose always.
molecules.alert: A hypo that doesn't clear after sugar and food is an emergency. Elderly patients and kidney disease need gentler choices.

molecules.simple: A DPP-4 inhibitor — it protects the gut's own GLP-1 signal so insulin is released smartly with meals and glucagon is tamed. Low hypoglycaemia risk, weight-neutral.
molecules.how: 100 mg once daily, with or without food; dose adjusts down in kidney disease.
molecules.alert: Report severe joint pain or pancreatitis signs (deep upper-belly pain radiating to back with vomiting) promptly.

molecules.simple: Another DPP-4 protector of the body's own meal-time insulin signal — same smart-release, low-hypo class as sitagliptin.
molecules.how: 50 mg once or twice daily regardless of meals.
molecules.alert: Liver disease needs caution and monitoring. Report persistent severe abdominal pain.

molecules.simple: An India-popular DPP-4 inhibitor in the same smart-insulin family — affordable and weight-neutral, often combined with metformin.
molecules.how: 20 mg once daily, with or without food.
molecules.alert: Report pancreatitis-like deep upper abdominal pain. Kidney impairment usually doesn't need dose change, but liver disease does.

molecules.simple: An SGLT2 inhibitor — it makes the kidneys spill extra sugar into urine. Sugar leaves, weight eases down, and the heart and kidneys get bonus protection.
molecules.how: One morning tablet, food optional. Drink adequate water; expect genital hygiene care since sugar-rich urine invites infections.
molecules.alert: Rare but serious: ketoacidosis WITHOUT very high sugar — nausea, vomiting, deep tiredness even with normal sugar means stop and test ketones/see a doctor. Skip the tablet on days of major surgery or severe illness.

molecules.simple: The other famous SGLT2 'sugar-in-urine' tablet with strong heart-failure trial results — prescribed for diabetes with heart or kidney protection in mind.
molecules.how: Morning tablet once daily; maintain fluids and genital hygiene.
molecules.alert: Same sick-day rule as dapagliflozin: pause during severe illness, vomiting or fasting; ketoacidosis signs need urgent care.

molecules.simple: A thiazolidinedione that makes fat, muscle and liver more sensitive to insulin. Effective and inexpensive, but it encourages fluid retention and weight gain.
molecules.how: 7.5–15 mg once daily with breakfast; effect builds over weeks.
molecules.alert: Not for heart failure patients — fluid can precipitate breathlessness. Bladder symptoms (blood in urine) need prompt evaluation.

molecules.simple: A starch-blocker that delays the gut enzyme breaking complex carbs into sugar — so post-meal sugar spikes flatten out instead of soaring.
molecules.how: Chew the tablet WITH the first bite of each meal; dose escalates slowly because gut gas is dose-related.
molecules.alert: If it causes a hypoglycaemia (rare, usually when combined with other drugs), ordinary sugar won't work — use glucose (Glucon-D), since it blocks table sugar breakdown.

molecules.simple: India's popular alpha-glucosidase blocker — same starch-slow-down idea as acarbose, blunting sugar spikes after Indian carb-heavy meals.
molecules.how: 0.2–0.3 mg chewed with the first mouthful of each meal.
molecules.alert: Same rule as acarbose for hypos: treat with pure glucose, not table sugar.

molecules.simple: A 24-hour 'basal' insulin released almost flat through the day — the background insulin the body always needs, injected once at the same time daily.
uses: Type 2 diabetes when tablets aren't enough
molecules.how: Injected subcutaneously (thigh/abdomen) once daily at a fixed hour; rotate sites. Doses come from the doctor — never self-adjust large steps.
molecules.alert: Any missed-meal hypo with confusion needs immediate glucose and help. Never share pens or needles; store unopened pens in the fridge.

molecules.simple: A rapid-acting 'mealtime' insulin that starts working in 10–15 minutes — injected right before eating to match the sugar load of that meal.
molecules.how: Injected 0–15 minutes before meals, dose matched to carbs as taught by the care team; rotate injection sites.
molecules.alert: If a pre-meal dose is taken but the meal is skipped, expect a hypo — carry glucose. Severe hypos with confusion are emergencies.

molecules.simple: A premixed insulin: 30% fast-acting for the meal plus 70% slow background — one injection covers both needs, common in cost-conscious Indian care.
molecules.how: Injected 30 minutes BEFORE meals (usually twice daily); the vial must be gently rolled to mix — never shaken hard.
molecules.alert: A severe hypo (confusion, collapse) is an emergency. Store in a fridge; opened vials at room temperature last ~28 days.

molecules.simple: The body's own thyroid hormone, made as a tablet — it restores metabolism in an underactive thyroid. Gentle, exact and lifelong for most who need it.
molecules.how: One tablet on a completely EMPTY stomach in the morning with water, then wait 30–60 minutes before tea/food (and keep 4 hours from calcium/iron). Same time daily; blood tests tune the dose.
watch: Palpitations or weight loss if the dose is too high
Usually none when dose is right
molecules.alert: Dose changes need TSH testing every 6–8 weeks. Chest pounding, tremor or severe sweating means the dose needs review — don't just stop.

molecules.simple: An anti-thyroid tablet that blocks the gland from over-producing hormone in hyperthyroidism/Graves' disease, calming the racing metabolism.
molecules.how: Dose starts high then tapers as the gland settles, under regular TFT blood tests; tablet swallowed whole with water.
molecules.alert: Sore throat with fever or mouth ulcers on this drug can signal a dangerous white-cell crash (agranulocytosis) — blood test the same day, don't wait.

molecules.simple: A corticosteroid — the body's own anti-inflammatory 'fire hose'. It calms severe allergy, asthma, arthritis and autoimmune flares, but has strong long-term side effects.
molecules.how: Morning dose after breakfast (matches the body's natural steroid rhythm); courses taper down on doctor's orders — NEVER stop abruptly after 2+ weeks.
molecules.alert: Sudden withdrawal after long use can cause collapse (adrenal crisis) — tapering is medical law. Carry a steroid card if on long therapy.

molecules.simple: A softer corticosteroid cousin of prednisolone — chosen for long courses (e.g., muscular dystrophy, nephrotic syndrome) because it disturbs weight and bones a bit less.
molecules.how: Morning dose after food; tapering rules are the same strict law as prednisolone.
molecules.alert: Never stop abruptly. Infections can smoulder silently on steroids — fever still needs a doctor's attention.

molecules.simple: A very potent steroid used for brain swelling, severe inflammation and in emergency care; the drops calm allergic eye inflammation.
molecules.how: Strictly as prescribed — potency means doses are tiny and courses short; eye drops follow the drop schedule strictly.
molecules.alert: Long or repeated courses need medical supervision; never self-continue leftover tablets.

molecules.simple: A middle-weight steroid used in short sharp courses (medrol dose packs) and as hospital pulses for nerve and kidney inflammation.
molecules.how: Tablets in the morning after food for a few days with taper; pulse injections are hospital-only.
molecules.alert: Same no-abrupt-stop rule. Blood sugar and BP rise during courses — diabetics monitor closely.

molecules.simple: A calcium-channel blocker that relaxes artery walls so blood flows with less push — lowering pressure gently over 24 hours, once a day.
molecules.how: One tablet daily at a fixed time, with or without food. Ankle puffiness is the classic effect — tell your doctor rather than stopping abruptly.
molecules.alert: Dizziness with fainting means BP has dipped too low — needs review. Never combine with sildenafil-type drugs without advice.

molecules.simple: An ARB — it blocks angiotensin, the hormone that tightens vessels, so arteries stay relaxed and pressure falls. Also protects kidneys in diabetes.
molecules.how: One tablet daily, with or without food. Kidney function and potassium are checked periodically.
molecules.alert: Strictly avoid in pregnancy — it can harm the baby. Combining with painkillers like diclofenac regularly can strain kidneys.

molecules.simple: The original ARB — blocks the vessel-tightening hormone angiotensin, easing pressure and shielding kidneys, especially in diabetics with protein leak.
molecules.how: 25–50 mg once or twice daily as prescribed; potassium-rich salt substitutes should be avoided unless advised.
molecules.alert: Avoid completely in pregnancy. Regular creatinine and potassium tests are part of therapy.

molecules.simple: A potent ARB blood-pressure tablet with 24-hour action, often the base of fixed combinations with amlodipine or a water pill.
molecules.how: 20–40 mg once daily, fixed time; blood tests monitor kidneys and potassium.
molecules.alert: Pregnancy is an absolute no. Persistent watery diarrhoea on long use (rare sprue-like enteropathy) must be reported.

molecules.simple: An ACE inhibitor — it stops angiotensin being formed at all. Protects the heart after a heart attack and slows diabetic kidney damage.
molecules.how: 2.5–10 mg once daily; a dry irritating cough is the class's known quirk — tell your doctor (switching to an ARB fixes it).
molecules.alert: Swelling of lips/tongue (angioedema) is a stop-immediately emergency. Avoid in pregnancy.

molecules.simple: An older ACE inhibitor that lowers pressure and eases the heart's workload in failure — affordable and well-studied.
molecules.how: 2.5–10 mg once or twice daily; keep potassium supplements and salt substitutes off unless advised.
molecules.alert: Face/lip swelling = emergency stop. Pregnancy contraindicated.

molecules.simple: A beta-blocker that slows and steadies the heart — used after heart attacks, for palpitations, BP and angina. It turns the heart's 'revving' down.
molecules.how: 25–100 mg daily in one or two doses; never stop suddenly — the heart can rebound (taper on doctor's advice).
molecules.alert: Pulse under ~50/min, fainting or severe breathlessness needs review. Diabetics: it can hide hypo warning signs.

molecules.simple: A highly heart-selective beta-blocker — the standard partner in heart-failure therapy, proven to help the weak pump work longer and steadier.
molecules.how: Once daily, started low and escalated by the doctor over weeks. Same never-stop-suddenly rule.
molecules.alert: Sudden breathlessness or pulse persistently below 50 needs assessment. Asthma patients need specialist judgement before beta-blockers.

molecules.simple: A classic beta-blocker for BP, palpitations and anxiety-related racing heart — long used, inexpensive, once daily.
molecules.how: 25–50 mg once daily; taper never-abrupt rule applies.
molecules.alert: Asthma can worsen — always disclose it. Combine cautiously with diltiazem/verapamil (pulse can drop dangerously).

molecules.simple: The non-selective beta-blocker — besides BP and palpitations it prevents migraine, steadies essential tremor and calms thyroid-related racing.
molecules.how: 10–40 mg two or three times daily as directed; tapering is required after long use.
molecules.alert: Never in asthma. Diabetics watch for masked hypos. Sudden stop can trigger rebound palpitations.

molecules.simple: A beta-blocker with extra vessel-relaxing action — a proven pillar of heart-failure treatment that eases both the pump and the pipes.
molecules.how: Taken with food, started tiny (3.125 mg) and escalated slowly by the doctor.
molecules.alert: Report worsening breathlessness or swelling in the first weeks — the dose may need slowing. Never stop abruptly.

molecules.simple: A gentle third-generation beta-blocker that also releases nitric oxide to relax vessels — fewer tiredness complaints than older blockers.
molecules.how: 2.5–5 mg once daily, food optional.
molecules.alert: Same taper rule. Severe asthma and heart block need specialist caution.

molecules.simple: A modern loop diuretic that flushes out salt and water — the workhorse for heart-failure swelling in legs and lungs, acting within the hour.
molecules.how: Morning dose (so sleep isn't disturbed by bathroom trips); potassium levels are monitored.
molecules.alert: Weigh yourself daily on diuretics — 2 kg jump in 3 days means congestion is building; call your doctor. Severe cramps or irregular heartbeat needs urgent potassium check.

molecules.simple: The classic loop diuretic for pulling fluid out fast — in lungs flooded by heart failure it is the emergency dewatering tool.
molecules.how: Morning tablet as prescribed; hospital injections act within minutes for emergencies.
molecules.alert: Daily weight and swelling checks matter; sudden weight gain or breathlessness lying flat needs same-day review.

molecules.simple: A potassium-sparing 'water tablet' that blocks aldosterone — remodels the stressed heart in failure and tames hormonal fluid retention and acne in PCOS.
molecules.how: 25–50 mg morning dose; potassium and creatinine are rechecked after starting — the doctor pairs it carefully with other drugs.
molecules.alert: Do NOT take potassium supplements or salt substitutes alongside without advice — dangerous potassium peaks.

molecules.simple: The classic thiazide water pill — modest salt-and-water loss that meaningfully lowers BP, often inside ARB combination tablets.
molecules.how: Morning dose; it slightly drops potassium and raises uric acid and sugar — blood tests track these.
molecules.alert: Gout patients beware — it raises uric acid. Severe weakness from low sodium/potassium needs urgent electrolytes.

molecules.simple: A statin — it blocks the liver's cholesterol factory, pulling LDL ('bad cholesterol') down and steadying artery plaques so they don't rupture into heart attacks.
molecules.how: One tablet at night (the liver makes cholesterol overnight), with or without food. It is a lifelong medicine once indicated, not a course.
molecules.alert: Dark urine + muscle weakness + fever together suggest rare muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) — stop and test immediately. Avoid grapefruit juice.

molecules.simple: The most potent common statin — biggest LDL drop per milligram, often chosen after heart attacks or when targets are strict.
molecules.how: One tablet evening/night; same lifelong rhythm as atorvastatin with periodic lipid and liver tests.
molecules.alert: Same muscle-danger rule as atorvastatin. Tell your doctor about all other medicines — interactions matter here.

molecules.simple: A triglyceride-lowering tablet — targets the 'fats' beyond cholesterol, often paired with a statin when both are high.
uses: Pancreatitis prevention in very high TG
molecules.how: One tablet daily with food; keep alcohol low (it fuels triglycerides).
watch: Muscle aches (more when combined with statin)
molecules.alert: Gallstones or severe kidney disease need caution. Muscle pain with dark urine = stop and test.

molecules.simple: A blood-platelet 'un-sticker' — keeps platelets from clumping inside stents and narrowed arteries. The anti-stroke and anti-stent-clot tablet.
molecules.how: One 75 mg tablet daily, with or without food — never skipped, since even 2 missed days raise stent-clot risk.
molecules.alert: Never start or stop it (or aspirin) around surgery/dental work without telling every doctor. Black stools or vomiting blood is an emergency.

molecules.simple: Micro-dose aspirin as a daily blood-platelet un-sticker — proven secondary prevention after heart attacks and strokes. Not started casually; bleeding risk is real.
molecules.how: One tablet after breakfast daily; the enteric-coated form reduces stomach contact.
molecules.alert: Black stools or any unusual heavy bleeding needs urgent care. Stop before surgery only on the operating team's advice.

molecules.simple: The emergency angina tablet that melts under the tongue, instantly widening coronary vessels to relieve chest pain within minutes.
molecules.how: At chest pain: sit down, place one tablet under the tongue; may repeat after 5 minutes, max 3 doses. If pain persists beyond 15 minutes — call an ambulance (it may be a heart attack).
molecules.alert: NEVER combine with sildenafil/tadalafil-type drugs — BP can collapse fatally. Always keep the tablet fresh (replaces every ~6 months).

molecules.simple: A long-acting nitrate cousin of nitroglycerin — keeps coronary arteries relaxed through the day to prevent angina attacks rather than treat them.
molecules.how: Morning dose (sometimes with a second midday one) — leaving an overnight nitrate-free window keeps it working; ER forms are once daily.
molecules.alert: Same absolute ban on sildenafil-type drugs. Low BP with fainting needs dose review.

molecules.simple: The classic anticoagulant — blocks vitamin-K clotting factors so blood flows past mechanical valves and clots more slowly. Doses are personalised by INR blood tests.
molecules.how: Same time daily; INR tests keep the dose in the safe band. Leafy greens, alcohol and many drugs swing its effect — consistency and communication matter.
molecules.alert: Blood in urine/stool, severe headache (brain bleed), or a fall with head injury = emergency. Pregnancy is contraindicated.

molecules.simple: A modern 'NOAC' blood thinner blocking factor Xa — no routine INR tests needed, fewer diet traps than warfarin, standard for atrial fibrillation and DVT today.
molecules.how: 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg twice when criteria say so); take with or without food — but never double up a missed dose.
molecules.alert: Any major unexplained bleeding, or a head injury while on it, is an emergency — tell every doctor you're on a blood thinner.

molecules.simple: Another factor-Xa blood thinner — once-daily dosing for most uses, widely used for DVT/PE treatment and AF stroke prevention.
molecules.how: Dose varies by indication — 20 mg once daily with the evening meal for AF; lower doses for some uses. Never self-adjust.
molecules.alert: Bleeding emergencies are managed exactly like apixaban — inform every clinician; a reversal agent exists in hospitals.

molecules.simple: A heavy-duty rhythm stabiliser for dangerous arrhythmias like atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia — powerful, but its long-term side effects need scheduled monitoring.
molecules.how: Usually a loading phase then a low maintenance tablet daily; lung, thyroid and liver tests run periodically.
molecules.alert: Breathlessness or dry cough on it can mean lung injury — report immediately. It interacts with warfarin and digoxin strongly.

molecules.simple: An old foxglove-derived medicine that strengthens the heart's squeeze and slows atrial fibrillation rates — still valuable in AF with heart failure.
molecules.how: Once daily, tiny dose, monitored by blood levels and kidney function; potassium balance matters.
molecules.alert: Yellow-tinted vision or halos are classic toxicity signs — report at once. It interacts with amiodarone and many diuretics.

molecules.simple: A pure heart-rate slowener — it works on the SA node's 'tick' without touching BP or contractility, added when rate stays high despite beta-blockers.
uses: Chronic heart failure with high pulse
molecules.how: Twice daily with food; doctor targets a resting pulse band (~50–60).
molecules.alert: Not for atrial fibrillation. Persistent pulse below 50 or new irregular rhythm needs ECG review.

molecules.simple: A calcium-channel blocker focused on the heart — slows a racing atrial rhythm and eases angina, while also relaxing vessels mildly.
molecules.how: SR forms once daily; regular forms 2–3 times a day. Combining with beta-blockers needs doctor supervision (pulse can over-slow).
molecules.alert: Heart block on ECG or fainting spells need review. Avoid grapefruit.

molecules.simple: An anti-anginal that teaches heart cells to burn fuel more efficiently under low oxygen — an add-on when angina persists despite standard drugs.
molecules.how: One 35 mg MR tablet twice daily with meals.
molecules.alert: Any tremor, rigidity or gait change on it means stop-and-review — it is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease.

molecules.simple: The classic combined birth-control pill — a low oestrogen plus a progestin that stops ovulation and thickens cervical mucus, giving reliable contraception when taken daily at the same time.
molecules.how: One pill daily at a fixed time from day 1 of the cycle; a missed pill is taken as soon as remembered (see pack rules). Smoking over 35 years old raises risks — disclose it.
molecules.alert: Severe leg calf pain/swelling, sudden breathlessness or one-sided weakness = possible clot — emergency. Migraine with aura contraindicates it.

molecules.simple: A modern combined pill whose progestin (drospirenone) counters water retention — often chosen for acne or bloating with contraception needs.
molecules.how: One tablet daily at a fixed time through the 21+7 pack schedule.
molecules.alert: Same clot warning as all combined pills. Potassium-raising drugs (ACE inhibitors) need caution with drospirenone.

molecules.simple: An anti-androgen pill — cyproterone blocks male-hormone effects while oestrogen cycles the uterus; the standard hormonal therapy for PCOS acne and excess hair growth.
molecules.how: One tablet daily from day 1 of the cycle, usually for months under gynaecological review; liver tests are monitored.
molecules.alert: Clot risk is slightly higher than plain pills — no smoking, report leg pain or breathlessness urgently. Not to be combined with other oestrogens.

molecules.simple: A progesterone-like hormone that prepares and steadies the uterine lining — famous in pregnancy-support and recurrent-miscarriage care, and for irregular cycles.
molecules.how: 10 mg once or twice daily as the gynaecologist schedules it — timing depends on the cycle day or pregnancy situation.
molecules.alert: Bleeding with pain in pregnancy always needs same-day examination, whatever the medicine.

molecules.simple: The body-identical progesterone hormone in capsule form — supports the uterine lining in early pregnancy, regulates cycles and aids luteal-phase support.
molecules.how: Orally at night (it causes drowsiness) or vaginally as instructed — the route matters, so follow the prescription exactly.
molecules.alert: Take at bedtime if dizziness occurs; never drive after a vaginal/oral high dose until you know your response.

molecules.simple: An ovulation-inducer — it tricks the brain into releasing more FSH so the ovary develops and releases an egg; the classic first tablet in infertility care.
molecules.how: Started day 2–5 of the cycle for 5 days under monitoring (follicular scans confirm response); never self-cycle without scans.
molecules.alert: Severe abdominal swelling and pain after the course can mean ovarian hyperstimulation — urgent gynaecological review. Multiple pregnancy risk rises.

molecules.simple: An aromatase blocker that lowers oestrogen — used for ovulation induction in PCOS (often ahead of clomiphene) and as hormonal therapy in breast cancer.
molecules.how: 2.5 mg daily for 5 cycle days (fertility) or daily long-term (oncology) — strictly per specialist.
molecules.alert: Bone density is monitored in long oncology use. Pregnancy must be excluded before fertility cycles.

molecules.simple: A clot-stabiliser — it stops the enzymes that dissolve fresh clots, so bleeding slows. The standard tablet for heavy periods and a hospital injection for trauma bleeding.
molecules.how: 1–1.5 g two or three times daily during heavy days of the period; injections are hospital-only.
molecules.alert: Not used with a history of clotting problems (DVT/stroke). Red-brown urine or leg swelling on it needs review.

molecules.simple: A period-pain pair: mefenamic calms the prostaglandin cramps while dicyclomine relaxes the uterine and gut muscle spasm — the two-hit approach to dysmenorrhoea.
molecules.how: One tablet up to three times daily during painful days, after food; syrup doses for girls are weight-based.
molecules.alert: Take after food (NSAID rule). Cramps that suddenly worsen or don't respond need a gynaecological check.

molecules.simple: Insulin-sensitising nutrient pair for PCOS — improves how the ovary and muscles respond to insulin, easing cycles, acne and metabolic markers over months.
molecules.how: One sachet (or tablet) daily, usually morning, for 3–6 months; works best alongside diet, exercise and weight goals.
molecules.alert: It's supportive, not a replacement for prescribed diabetes or fertility therapy. Cycle changes should be reviewed by a gynaecologist.

molecules.simple: Vitamin B9 — the pre-pregnancy essential. Adequate folate in the first weeks of pregnancy prevents neural-tube defects in the baby; it also supports red-cell production.
molecules.how: 0.4–0.8 mg daily when planning pregnancy (from at least a month before); 5 mg doses are for deficiency or special cases.
molecules.alert: Never use the 5 mg tablet casually as a multivitamin — doses should match the purpose.

molecules.simple: A dopamine agonist that switches off prolactin — restarts cycles and fertility when a prolactin-secreting pituitary problem has shut them down.
molecules.how: Low doses twice weekly initially, titrated to prolactin levels; taken with food at night.
molecules.alert: Report new urges or compulsions (rare behavioural effect), breathlessness or chest pain on long use — heart valves are monitored.

molecules.simple: The sunshine vitamin — it lets the gut absorb calcium and keeps bones, muscles and immunity supplied. Indian indoor lifestyles make deficiency extremely common.
molecules.how: Weekly 60,000 IU sachet with milk for 6–8 weeks (doctor-planned), then a maintenance dose; daily 1,000–2,000 IU is the common maintenance.
molecules.alert: More is NOT better — unsupervised megadoses for months can raise calcium dangerously (thirst, confusion, stones). Follow the schedule.

molecules.simple: The bone-building pair — calcium as the building block plus vitamin D so the calcium is actually absorbed. Standard in pregnancy, teens, and osteoporosis care.
molecules.how: One tablet after lunch or dinner (split from levothyroxine, iron and tetracyclines by 4 hours — they block each other).
molecules.alert: Kidney-stone formers and high blood calcium need medical dosing. Spread doses — the gut absorbs ~500 mg at a time best.

molecules.simple: The nerve-and-energy vitamin trio — B1, B6 and B12 keep nerves insulated, blood cells forming and metabolism humming; deficiencies show as tingling, fatigue and mouth sores.
molecules.how: One tablet/capsule daily after food; injections are given for severe deficiency.
molecules.alert: High-dose B6 taken for months can paradoxically damage nerves — stick to label doses.

molecules.simple: The active form of B12 — the nerve-repair and blood-making vitamin. Vegetarians, metformin users and the elderly are the usual deficient groups.
molecules.how: One tablet daily after food, or weekly injections for severe deficiency, under blood-test guidance.
molecules.alert: Numbness that persists needs proper neurological workup — B12 is not a cure-all for every tingling.

molecules.simple: The citrus vitamin — needed to build collagen, heal wounds and keep immunity supplied; deficiency shows as bleeding gums and slow healing.
molecules.how: One chewable tablet daily, ideally with or after food; extra vitamin C doesn't cure colds but supports general needs.
molecules.alert: Kidney-stone formers should avoid megadoses — oxalate stones can be encouraged.

molecules.simple: A one-a-day safety net of essential vitamins with zinc for immunity and wound healing — useful in poor intake, recovery illness, and picky diets.
molecules.how: One tablet daily after breakfast; courses of 1–3 months are typical.
watch: Mild nausea if taken empty stomach
molecules.alert: Not a substitute for diagnosing real fatigue — persistent weakness needs tests, not just supplements.

molecules.simple: A gentle modern iron with vitamin C built in for absorption, plus folate for blood-cell building — the standard pregnancy and anaemia prescription.
molecules.how: One tablet daily on an empty-ish stomach with water or citrus (NOT with milk, tea or calcium — they block iron). Stools turn black: normal.
molecules.alert: Haemoglobin is rechecked after 4–6 weeks; if it hasn't risen, causes beyond iron are investigated. Keep away from children — iron overdose is toxic.

molecules.simple: The classic iron-folate capsule used in national anaemia programmes — effective, economical, with the usual iron stomach rules.
molecules.how: One capsule daily with citrus juice, away from tea/coffee and calcium by 2 hours.
molecules.alert: Recheck haemoglobin in 4–6 weeks. Children must never access iron capsules.

molecules.simple: A fat-soluble antioxidant vitamin — protects cell membranes from oxidation; used in deficiency states, some skin conditions and nerve support.
molecules.how: One capsule daily with a meal containing fat for absorption.
molecules.alert: High-dose long-term E has been linked to bleeding tendency — don't megadose without advice.

molecules.simple: The immunity-and-healing mineral — required for hundreds of enzymes, taste, wound repair and infection defence; WHO gives zinc in childhood diarrhoea.
molecules.how: 20 mg once daily for 14 days in childhood diarrhoea; adults 25–50 mg short courses as advised.
molecules.alert: Months of high-dose zinc can deplete copper and cause nerve symptoms — supplementation should be time-bounded.

molecules.simple: A bisphosphonate that slows the cells dissolving bone, tipping the balance back to bone-building — the standard osteoporosis treatment after fractures or on steroids.
molecules.how: One weekly 70 mg tablet: on waking, EMPTY stomach, with a full glass of plain water, sitting/standing upright 30 minutes, no food or other pills — the ritual protects the oesophagus.
molecules.alert: Chest pain on swallowing means stop and call. Jaw bone issues are rare but dental work should be mentioned to the dentist.

molecules.simple: Another weekly bisphosphonate for osteoporosis — same bone-resorption slowdown, alternative when alendronate doesn't suit.
molecules.how: Weekly tablet with water on an empty stomach, upright for 30 minutes — identical ritual to alendronate.
molecules.alert: Same oesophagus-protection rules; dental team should know you're on it.

molecules.simple: The once-a-year IV bisphosphonate — one hospital drip strengthens bones for months, ideal when weekly tablets are forgotten or poorly tolerated.
molecules.how: Given as a slow IV infusion by staff with hydration and dental checks beforehand; yearly for osteoporosis.
watch: Flu-like aches and fever for 1–2 days after (common)
molecules.alert: Kidney disease dosing is specialist territory; jaw health review before therapy is standard.

molecules.simple: A parathyroid-hormone fragment that is the only true bone-BUILDER — used for severe osteoporosis with fractures, daily self-injected for up to 2 years.
molecules.how: One daily subcutaneous injection into thigh/abdomen; cold-chain storage; courses capped at 24 months then followed by a bisphosphonate.
molecules.alert: Avoid in prior bone cancer or raised calcium. Sit or lie down briefly after the first doses if dizzy.

molecules.simple: The ACTIVE form of vitamin D — used when kidneys can't convert ordinary vitamin D themselves (CKD, hypoparathyroidism). Calcium levels are watched closely.
molecules.how: 0.25–0.5 mcg daily as titrated by blood calcium levels; taken with calcium as instructed.
watch: Thirst and excess urination if calcium rises
molecules.alert: Overdose risk is real (unlike plain vitamin D) — never self-escalate; periodic calcium blood tests are mandatory.

molecules.simple: Cartilage building-block supplements — evidence is modest, but many knee-osteoarthritis patients report smoother joints over 2–3 months of use.
molecules.how: One tablet twice or thrice daily with meals for at least 2–3 months before judging benefit.
molecules.alert: Shellfish-derived products need allergy disclosure. Diabetics monitor sugars initially. It eases symptoms — it doesn't rebuild lost cartilage.

molecules.simple: The classic anti-histamine — blocks the histamine that causes sneezing, itching and runny nose. Mildly drowsy for some, fast-acting for most.
molecules.how: One 10 mg tablet at night; take at bedtime if it makes you sleepy. For hives it may be used up to twice daily on doctor's advice.
molecules.alert: Avoid alcohol and driving until you know your response. Hives with lip/tongue swelling or breathing trouble is an emergency (anaphylaxis), not a tablet situation.

molecules.simple: The refined active half of cetirizine — same allergy relief with a slightly lighter drowsiness profile at half the milligrams.
molecules.how: 5 mg once daily in the evening.
molecules.alert: Same anaphylaxis warning — swelling of airway structures is an emergency.

molecules.simple: A non-drowsy second-generation anti-histamine — daytime hay fever relief without the fog, taken once daily.
molecules.how: 120–180 mg once daily with water (not fruit juice — apple/orange juice cuts absorption).
molecules.alert: Hives plus airway swelling is an emergency regardless of tablets.

molecules.simple: A leukotriene blocker — stops one of the allergy/asthma chemical cascades rather than histamine. A once-nightly tablet that prevents asthma symptoms and allergic rhinitis.
molecules.how: One tablet at bedtime; it is a PREVENTER — taken daily, not as rescue during an attack.
molecules.alert: Rare mood changes, vivid dreams, irritability or agitation — report to the doctor; dose review may be needed.

molecules.simple: The double-blocker combo for stubborn allergic rhinitis: leukotriene cascade plus histamine receptor in one bedtime tablet.
uses: Dust allergy not settling on single drugs
molecules.how: One tablet at night after food.
molecules.alert: Same mood-change note as montelukast; anaphylaxis never waits for tablets.

molecules.simple: The old-school anti-histamine — very effective for itching and sneezing, but reliably sleepy, which is why it's dosed at night or used in cough-cold combos.
molecules.how: 4 mg at bedtime, or as directed in combination products.
molecules.alert: Not for infants without advice; caution in glaucoma and prostate trouble. Never drive after a dose.

molecules.simple: An anti-histamine with calming properties — used for itchy skin conditions and for anxiety-related restlessness under supervision.
molecules.how: 10–25 mg up to three times daily as prescribed; strongly sedating in many people.
molecules.alert: It can lengthen the heart's QT interval with other drugs — disclose all medicines. Never combine with alcohol.

molecules.simple: The rescue bronchodilator — within minutes it flings open tightened airway muscles, ending an asthma attack's breathlessness. Every asthma patient carries one.
molecules.how: Inhaler: 2 puffs during an attack (spacer improves delivery); nebuliser solution for children/severe cases. If puffs are needed more than twice a week, the PREVENTER needs review.
molecules.alert: An attack not relieved by repeated puffs, with bluish lips or speech-breaking breathlessness, is a medical emergency — hospital now.

molecules.simple: An inhaled steroid preventer — calms airway inflammation at the source so attacks don't start. The daily 'brush your teeth' medicine of asthma.
molecules.how: Inhaled daily at fixed times; rinse the mouth after every use to prevent thrush. Never used as rescue during an attack.
watch: Oral thrush if mouth not rinsed
molecules.alert: Stopping it because 'I feel fine' is how attacks return — preventers are continued on schedule.

molecules.simple: Steroid preventer plus a fast long-acting bronchodilator in one inhaler — both calms inflammation daily and opens airways quickly when needed.
molecules.how: Regular scheduled puffs (often 2 twice daily); some regimens also allow it as the reliever — only if your doctor has taught that SMART plan.
molecules.alert: Attack not settling despite the inhaler plan = emergency. Don't exceed prescribed daily caps.

molecules.simple: Another steroid-plus-long-acting-dilator combo inhaler — the daily maintenance pair that keeps asthma and COPD airways quiet.
molecules.how: Scheduled puffs twice daily with mouth rinse after; NOT a rescue inhaler.
molecules.alert: Increasing rescue-puff use means the control plan needs review — see your doctor rather than pushing the inhaler.

molecules.simple: A dual nebulised bronchodilator — two different airway-openers (anticholinergic + beta-agonist) for stronger relief in wheezing episodes and COPD.
molecules.how: One respule via nebuliser as prescribed, 3–4 times daily in acute phases.
molecules.alert: Nebs that stop helping, or drowsiness with worsening breathing, mean hospital — don't keep repeating at home.

molecules.simple: A theophylline-family bronchodilator with fewer jittery side effects — an oral add-on for chronic wheeze when inhalers alone don't hold the line.
molecules.how: 200–400 mg twice daily after food.
molecules.alert: Heart-rhythm problems need caution; report chest flutters or sleeplessness.

molecules.simple: A mucolytic — it thins sticky phlegm so coughs clear it more easily, turning a dry rattling cough into a productive, clearing one.
molecules.how: 30 mg two or three times daily after food, with plenty of warm fluids.
molecules.alert: Cough beyond 3 weeks, blood-streaked sputum, fever with breathlessness — needs a chest evaluation, not more syrup.

molecules.simple: The classic 'Ascoril' trio: opens airways, thins phlegm and lubricates the cough — for chesty congested coughs with wheeze.
molecules.how: 5–10 ml three times daily as prescribed; sedation possible, so school/work caution.
molecules.alert: Not for infants under guidance. Blood in sputum or high fever needs a chest exam.

molecules.simple: The cold-relief trio: anti-histamine for sneezing, decongestant for blocked nose, paracetamol for fever and headache — the 'sinus tablet' of Indian chemists.
molecules.how: One tablet two or three times daily for 3–4 days maximum, after food.
molecules.alert: Not with other paracetamol products (double-dosing risk). BP patients should ask before decongestants.

molecules.simple: A steroid spray that shrinks nasal-lining inflammation at the source — the most effective regular treatment for blocked, itchy allergic noses.
molecules.how: One–two sprays per nostril daily, aimed slightly outward (away from the septum), best started BEFORE allergy season and used regularly.
molecules.alert: Nosebleeds repeatedly or crusting — pause and review. Steroid sprays act over days, not instantly.

molecules.simple: A fast decongestant spray that shrinks swollen nasal blood vessels in seconds — marvellous for 3 days, dangerous beyond that.
molecules.how: One spray per nostril at night for a MAXIMUM of 3–5 days.
molecules.alert: Longer use causes rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) — the nose blocks worse without it. Never in infants under advice.

molecules.simple: The oral steroid burst for serious asthma/allergy flares — a few days of tablets to break the inflammation cycle while inhalers resume control.
molecules.how: Doctor-planned burst (often 5–7 days) with taper if longer; morning dose after food.
molecules.alert: Never stop long courses abruptly. Repeat flare cycles mean the maintenance plan needs redesign.

molecules.simple: A mast-cell stabiliser with anti-histamine action — used as a slow-build preventer in allergic children and as soothing anti-allergy eye drops.
molecules.how: 1 mg at bedtime (it sedates); eye drops twice daily in the affected eyes.
molecules.alert: It is a preventer — don't expect instant relief. Eye pain or vision change needs an eye doctor, not just drops.

molecules.simple: The standard anti-fungal — it punches holes in fungal cell walls. The cream for ringworm and athlete's foot, drops for fungal ear infection.
molecules.how: Thin cream layer twice daily, and continue 1–2 WEEKS after the rash disappears — stopping early is why ringworm returns. Keep folds dry.
molecules.alert: Rash spreading fast with fever needs a doctor (could be bacterial). Face or scalp ringworm needs oral treatment, not cream alone.

molecules.simple: A stronger anti-fungal family member — the shampoo for stubborn dandruff and seborrhoea, cream for ringworm and tinea versicolor patches.
molecules.how: Shampoo twice weekly: lather, wait 5 minutes, rinse. Cream twice daily for 2–4 weeks.
molecules.alert: Oral ketoconazole tablets are no longer used (liver risk) — stick to external forms. Eye contact should be avoided.

molecules.simple: The strongest common oral anti-fungal — actually kills the fungus rather than just suppressing it; the treatment for nail fungus and stubborn ringworm.
molecules.how: 250 mg once daily for weeks (toenails need 12+ weeks); cream twice daily for local infection. Liver tests for long courses.
molecules.alert: Liver disease needs caution and monitoring. Taste loss during the course must be reported.

molecules.simple: A topical antibiotic ointment that kills staph and strep on the skin — the standard for infected cuts, boils in early stage and impetigo sores.
molecules.how: Small amount three times daily on the cleaned area for 5–10 days, or a pea-sized amount inside nostrils twice daily for carrier decolonisation.
molecules.alert: Spreading redness with fever means the infection has gone deeper — needs oral antibiotics, not ointment.

molecules.simple: A two-antibiotic surface shield for minor cuts and grazes — covers the common skin germs while the wound heals.
molecules.how: Thin layer 1–3 times daily on cleaned skin.
molecules.alert: Rash worsening rather than settling means allergy — stop. Deep, dirty or animal wounds need proper wound care and tetanus review.

molecules.simple: A super-potent steroid cream for thick, stubborn plaques like psoriasis and severe eczema — powerful medicine with strict short-course rules.
molecules.how: Thin layer ONCE or twice daily for a maximum of 2 weeks on the same patch, then reviewed — potent steroids thin skin with overuse.
molecules.alert: Never on the face, groin or folds unless a dermatologist directs. Never use leftover clobetasol casually for any itch.

molecules.simple: The gentle everyday steroid cream — takes the itch and redness out of mild eczema, insect bites and rashes without the strong-steroid risks.
molecules.how: Thin layer twice daily for up to 1–2 weeks on small areas.
molecules.alert: If a rash isn't clearly better in 7 days, get it diagnosed instead of continuing blindly. Not for fungal areas (they worsen with steroids).

molecules.simple: The scabies killer — a nerve poison to mites, safe for humans. Applied as a full-body overnight coat for everyone in the household at once.
molecules.how: Apply from neck-down to the WHOLE body (including soles, between fingers) at night, wash off after 8–14 hours; repeat once after 7 days. Treat all family members simultaneously; wash clothes/bedding hot.
watch: Itching can persist 2–4 weeks after cure (post-scabies itch)
molecules.alert: Continuous new burrows/blisters after two proper applications needs review — maybe crusted scabies requiring oral therapy.

molecules.simple: The definitive severe-acne drug — it shrinks the skin's oil glands, unclogging the root cause. Very effective, very rule-bound, always dermatologist-supervised.
molecules.how: 0.5–1 mg/kg daily in divided doses with fatty food for 4–6+ month courses, with monthly blood tests (lipids, liver) during therapy.
molecules.alert: ABSOLUTE: causes severe birth defects — pregnancy prevention is mandatory through the course and a month after. Mood changes must be reported immediately.

molecules.simple: The nightly acne duo-gel: adapalene renews pore lining while benzoyl peroxide kills acne bacteria — together clearing comedones and pimples.
molecules.how: Pea-sized amount for the WHOLE face at night on dry skin, 2–3 nights weekly at first, building to nightly; moisturise mornings and use sunscreen.
molecules.alert: Benzoyl peroxide bleaches fabrics and hair. Strong irritation means space out applications rather than quitting.

molecules.simple: A steroid-free immune-calming ointment for delicate areas — face, eyelids, folds — where strong steroids are unsafe in eczema and vitiligo protocols.
molecules.how: Thin layer twice daily on affected areas; brief burning at first application usually settles in days.
molecules.alert: Avoid intense sun exposure on treated areas; not for infected skin.

molecules.simple: A broad antibiotic drop for bacterial conjunctivitis — pink eye with sticky discharge — hitting the common eye germs in four daily doses.
molecules.how: One drop 3–4 times daily for about a week, as prescribed; never share the bottle.
molecules.alert: Steroid-containing eye drops need an eye doctor's direction. Vision drop, severe pain or light sensitivity is same-day ophthalmology territory.

molecules.simple: A beta-blocker eye drop that reduces fluid production inside the eye — the classic glaucoma pressure-lowering drop, usually twice daily.
molecules.how: One drop twice daily, pressing the inner corner briefly after instilling (reduces body absorption).
watch: Rarely slow pulse or asthma-like wheeze (body absorption)
molecules.alert: Asthma and heart-block patients must tell the ophthalmologist. Missed glaucoma drops quietly damage vision — adherence matters.

molecules.simple: Artificial tears — a protective lubricant layer for dry, screen-tired eyes. Preservative-free forms are gentlest for frequent use.
molecules.how: One drop in each eye as needed — even 4–6 times daily for preservative-free versions.
molecules.alert: Eye pain, redness with light sensitivity or vision loss is NOT dryness — see an eye doctor.

molecules.simple: An anti-histamine-plus-stabiliser eye drop for itchy allergic eyes — relieves the itch within minutes and calms the mast cells that keep it flaring.
uses: Itchy watery eyes in pollen/dust season
molecules.how: One drop twice daily during the allergy period.
molecules.alert: Vision change or pain needs ophthalmology. Don't share drop bottles between family members.

molecules.simple: Soothing medicated lozenges for a scratchy throat — local antiseptic plus mild anaesthetic that numbs pain while saliva washes the inflamed lining.
molecules.how: Dissolve one lozenge slowly every 2–3 hours as needed; don't chew or swallow whole.
molecules.alert: Fever with white patches on tonsils, or sore throat beyond 5 days, needs a strep assessment — lozenges don't treat strep.

molecules.simple: A first-line antidepressant — it raises serotonin signalling gradually, lifting low mood, panic and obsessive loops over 2–4 weeks. One of the safest, most-prescribed mind medicines.
molecules.how: Morning dose after food, starting low and stepped up by the doctor. It builds over weeks — stopping it early is the commonest failure. Taper slowly when discontinuing.
molecules.alert: Any new suicidal thoughts, especially in young adults early in treatment, need immediate contact with the doctor. Never mix with linezolid or tramadol (serotonin surge risk).

molecules.simple: A clean, well-tolerated SSRI antidepressant for depression and anxiety — often chosen for fewer drug interactions and gentler side-effect profile.
molecules.how: 5–10 mg morning or night; benefit over 2–4 weeks; taper on discontinuation.
molecules.alert: QT heart-interval caution at higher doses in heart patients. Same urgent-contact rule for worsening mood.

molecules.simple: The original SSRI with a long half-life (missed doses forgive you) — used for depression, OCD, bulimia and PMDD.
molecules.how: Morning dose (it energises some people); 20 mg typical adult dose, adjusted by the doctor.
molecules.alert: Long half-life means washout periods matter when switching drugs — specialist territory. Worsening mood needs immediate contact.

molecules.simple: A serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor — lifts mood AND dampens nerve pain, making it the dual-use tablet for depression with diabetic nerve or chronic pain.
molecules.how: Once daily, swallow whole (DR capsule); can be taken with or without food.
molecules.alert: Liver disease is a contraindication. Abrupt stop causes zappy discontinuation effects — taper always.

molecules.simple: An antidepressant that works on a different axis — noradrenaline and serotonin via blocking — famous for restoring appetite and deep sleep, often chosen when weight loss and insomnia accompany depression.
uses: Depression with insomnia and poor appetite
molecules.how: Bedtime dose; sedation is strongest at LOW doses (7.5–15 mg) and eases as dose rises — counterintuitive but true.
molecules.alert: Report unusual bruising (rare blood-count effect). Combination with other sedatives stacks drowsiness.

molecules.simple: The old tricyclic — at tiny doses it's a nerve-pain and migraine-prevention workhorse; at higher doses, a classic antidepressant. Sleepy, so it lives at bedtime.
molecules.how: 10–25 mg at night, titrated slowly; the analgesic effect works at far smaller doses than the antidepressant one.
molecules.alert: Overdose is dangerous with tricyclics — keep quantity limited and away from impulsive access. Heart-rhythm patients need ECG review.

molecules.simple: A fast-acting benzodiazepine for acute panic and severe anxiety spikes — quietens the brain's alarm within the hour. A short-term rescue, not a long-term plan.
molecules.how: 0.25–0.5 mg as prescribed, at most short courses — dependence builds within weeks of daily use, so doctors keep it time-boxed.
molecules.alert: Never combine with alcohol or opioids — breathing can stop. Abrupt stop after daily use causes seizures; tapering is mandatory.

molecules.simple: A longer-acting benzodiazepine that steadies both seizure activity and severe panic — also used in restless legs and certain twitching disorders.
molecules.how: Dose at bedtime usually, titrated slowly; long-term use needs deliberate taper plans.
molecules.alert: Same dependence and tapering law as alprazolam. Sudden stop can trigger seizures.

molecules.simple: A thienodiazepine popular in Indian practice for anxiety and insomnia — quicker clear-headedness for many users, with the same dependence rules as benzodiazepines.
molecules.how: 0.25–1 mg at night or as prescribed; short courses only.
molecules.alert: Dependence and withdrawal risks are real — never self-extend daily use. No alcohol.

molecules.simple: A sleep-onset tablet — quiets brain activity just enough to fall asleep, without the morning hangover of older sleeping pills. Strictly a bedside-then-bed medicine.
molecules.how: 5–10 mg at bedtime with nothing else planned — take it IN bed, because some people do complex things (sleepwalking, texting) with no memory of it.
molecules.alert: Complex sleep behaviours (walking, eating, driving asleep) mean stop and report. Combining with alcohol is dangerous.
